questions.question: What is NoSQL and why was it created?
questions.answer: NoSQL ('Not Only SQL') is a category of database systems that don't use traditional relational tables. It was created because internet-scale applications needed to handle unstructured data, flexible schemas, and horizontal scaling that SQL databases couldn't efficiently support. Applications like social media, streaming, and e-commerce drove the need for databases that could scale to millions of concurrent users.

questions.question: What are the four types of NoSQL databases? Give an example of each.
questions.answer: 1) Key-Value Stores (Redis, DynamoDB/ElastiCache) — simple key→value lookup, great for caching and sessions. 2) Document Stores (MongoDB, Amazon DocumentDB) — flexible JSON documents, great for user profiles and CMS. 3) Wide-Column Stores (Cassandra, Amazon Keyspaces) — column-family storage, great for IoT and time-series. 4) Graph Databases (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune) — nodes and edges, great for social networks and fraud detection.

questions.question: What is Amazon DynamoDB and what makes it different from RDS?
questions.answer: DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed, serverless NoSQL database delivering single-digit millisecond performance at any scale. Unlike RDS (relational), DynamoDB has a flexible schema (items can have different attributes), scales horizontally to unlimited throughput, requires no server management, and is optimised for simple access patterns. RDS supports complex SQL queries and JOINs; DynamoDB does not.

questions.question: What is a Primary Key in DynamoDB? What are the two types?
questions.answer: A Primary Key uniquely identifies each item in a DynamoDB table. Type 1: Simple Primary Key — uses only a Partition Key, which must be unique across all items. Type 2: Composite Primary Key — uses a Partition Key + Sort Key. Items can share the same Partition Key but must have unique Sort Keys. The combination of both must be unique.

questions.question: What is AWS DMS and what is it used for?
questions.answer: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) is a fully managed service that migrates databases to AWS with minimal downtime. It creates a managed replication instance that reads from a source endpoint and writes to a target endpoint. It's used for moving on-premises databases to AWS, upgrading database versions, migrating from commercial to open-source databases, and continuous replication for analytics pipelines.

questions.question: What is AWS Lambda and how does it work?
questions.answer: Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs code in response to events without managing servers. You upload your function code, define a trigger (API Gateway, S3, DynamoDB Streams, CloudWatch Events, etc.), and Lambda automatically executes the code when the trigger fires. It scales automatically from zero to thousands of concurrent executions and you pay only for the compute time used.

questions.question: What is the difference between Eventually Consistent and Strongly Consistent reads in DynamoDB?
questions.answer: Eventually Consistent reads (default) may return slightly stale data immediately after a write, as DynamoDB replicates across 3 AZs and the read might hit a replica not yet updated. They cost 0.5 RCUs per 4KB. Strongly Consistent reads always return the most current data (reads the latest from all replicas) and cost 1 full RCU per 4KB. Strongly Consistent reads are NOT supported on GSIs or Global Tables.

questions.question: What are the three DMS migration task types?
questions.answer: 1) Full Load: Migrates all existing data in a single pass. Requires source downtime at cutover. 2) Full Load + CDC: Migrates all existing data AND continuously captures/applies ongoing changes using Change Data Capture. Enables near-zero downtime migration. 3) CDC Only: Only replicates ongoing changes from the source, assuming the target already has the base data loaded via another method.

questions.question: What is the maximum timeout and memory range for Lambda functions?
questions.answer: Maximum timeout: 15 minutes per invocation. Memory range: 128 MB minimum to 10,240 MB (10 GB) maximum. CPU is allocated proportionally to memory — doubling memory also doubles CPU. The Lambda free tier includes 1 million requests/month and 400,000 GB-seconds/month — and this free tier does NOT expire.

questions.question: What is Change Data Capture (CDC) in DMS?
questions.answer: CDC is a technique where DMS reads the source database's transaction logs in real-time, capturing every insert, update, and delete operation. These changes are continuously applied to the target database, keeping both in sync during the migration window. This is what enables near-zero-downtime migrations — the source stays live while the target catches up, and cutover happens at a chosen moment.

questions.question: Scenario: Your company's Oracle database (10 years of data, 2TB) needs to move to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with zero downtime. Walk me through your approach.
questions.answer: (Situation) 2TB Oracle database, cannot afford downtime, different database engines. (Task) Migrate with zero downtime and no data loss. (Action) Step 1: Use AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to convert Oracle schema — tables, stored procedures, triggers — to Aurora PostgreSQL format. Review SCT report and manually fix flagged objects. Step 2: Create DMS replication instance, configure Oracle as source endpoint and Aurora as target. Step 3: Run Full Load + CDC migration — DMS copies all 2TB while CDC captures ongoing Oracle writes. Step 4: Monitor replication lag in DMS console until lag reaches near-zero. Step 5: At cutover window, stop writes to Oracle, let remaining CDC catch up, switch application connection strings to Aurora. (Result) Zero data loss, minimal downtime (minutes at cutover, not hours).

questions.question: Scenario: A user reports that the first API request after the app is idle for 10 minutes takes 2 seconds, but all subsequent requests take 50ms. The stack is API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Lambda function behind API Gateway serving a DynamoDB-backed API. First request after idle period is 40x slower. (Task) Diagnose and eliminate the latency spike. (Action) This is a cold start — Lambda initialised a new execution environment including loading the Node.js/Python runtime, the function code, and establishing the DynamoDB connection. The fix is Provisioned Concurrency: pre-warm a defined number of Lambda instances so they are always ready to handle requests without initialisation delay. Alternatively, move DynamoDB connection initialization outside the handler function (to the global scope) so it persists across warm invocations. (Result) Cold starts eliminated for latency-sensitive requests; cold start cost offset by improved user experience.

questions.question: Scenario: Your team is building a real-time leaderboard for a mobile game with 5 million daily active users. Players earn points continuously. The leaderboard must update within seconds and return the top 100 players instantly. Which database would you use and how would you design it?
questions.answer: (Situation) High-frequency writes (points updates), high-frequency reads (top-100 queries), real-time requirements. (Task) Design a database solution for a live leaderboard. (Action) Use DynamoDB with a GSI. Table design: Partition Key = 'LEADERBOARD' (all items in one logical group), Sort Key = PlayerID. Create a GSI with Partition Key = 'LEADERBOARD' and Sort Key = Score (numeric) — this allows querying the top 100 by scanning the GSI in descending score order. Alternatively, use Amazon ElastiCache (Redis) with a Sorted Set — ZADD for score updates, ZREVRANGE for top-N queries in O(log N) time. Redis Sorted Sets are the canonical leaderboard solution for sub-millisecond response. (Result) Sub-10ms leaderboard reads even under millions of concurrent users.

questions.question: Scenario: Your Lambda function needs to query an RDS database on every invocation. You notice DB connections are exhausted during traffic spikes. How do you solve this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Lambda scales to thousands of concurrent instances. Each instance creates a new DB connection. RDS has a connection limit (e.g., 500). (Task) Prevent connection exhaustion while maintaining Lambda scalability. (Action) Use Amazon RDS Proxy — it sits between Lambda and RDS, maintaining a warm pool of database connections. Lambda connects to RDS Proxy, which multiplexes thousands of Lambda connections down to a small pool of actual RDS connections. Also move the DB connection initialisation outside the Lambda handler (in the global scope) so connections are reused across warm invocations. (Result) Connection count stays within RDS limits regardless of Lambda concurrency.

questions.question: Scenario: You accidentally delete 10,000 items from a DynamoDB table in production. How do you recover?
questions.answer: (Situation) Accidental mass deletion from a production DynamoDB table. (Task) Recover the deleted items with minimal data loss. (Action) If Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) was enabled: use DynamoDB PITR to restore the table to a specific point in time before the deletion — this restores to a new table, then copy data back to the original. If PITR was not enabled, check for DynamoDB Streams — if streams were enabled, the delete events were captured; you can use the stream records to reconstruct what was deleted. If neither was enabled, restore from the most recent on-demand backup if one exists. Going forward: always enable PITR (costs ~20% of storage) and set up automated backups. (Result) Data recovery with acceptable RPO depending on available recovery mechanisms.

questions.question: Scenario: The team wants to process every new S3 upload (CSV files) through a data validation Lambda and store results in DynamoDB. Design the event-driven architecture.
questions.answer: (Situation) CSV files uploaded to S3 must be validated automatically and results stored in DynamoDB. (Task) Design a fully automated, event-driven pipeline. (Action) Configure S3 Event Notifications on the source bucket to trigger a Lambda function on 's3:ObjectCreated:*' events. The Lambda function: reads the CSV from S3 using the event's bucket and key, validates each row against business rules, writes valid records to DynamoDB with partition key = filename + timestamp, writes validation summary (total rows, passed, failed) to a separate DynamoDB table for audit. For error handling, add a Dead Letter Queue (SQS or SNS) on the Lambda to capture failed invocations. (Result) Zero-infrastructure pipeline — scales to unlimited file volume, zero cost when idle.

questions.question: Scenario: Your DMS migration task is running but the target database is 6 hours behind the source. What could cause this and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) DMS CDC replication lag is 6 hours and growing. (Task) Identify the bottleneck and reduce lag. (Action) Investigate these causes in order: 1) Replication instance is undersized — upgrade to a larger instance class (more CPU/RAM). 2) Source is high-write — DMS is processing more changes than it can apply; enable parallel apply on the task settings. 3) Target database is the bottleneck — check target RDS CPU and IOPS, scale up or enable Multi-AZ. 4) Network bandwidth — check VPC routing, use a Direct Connect or VPN for large-volume migrations. 5) LOB columns (large objects) — configure DMS LOB handling settings appropriately. Monitor the 'CDCLatencySource' and 'CDCLatencyTarget' CloudWatch metrics to isolate which side has the lag. (Result) Replication lag reduced to under 5 seconds, ready for cutover.

questions.question: Scenario: You deployed the Job Application project and it works locally but the React frontend shows 'Network Error' when submitting the form on EC2. What do you check first?
questions.answer: (Situation) React form submission fails with Network Error on EC2 but worked locally. (Task) Debug the connection failure between frontend and backend. (Action) Check in order: 1) Security Group rules — is port 5000 open in the EC2 Security Group's inbound rules for 0.0.0.0/0? 2) Is the Node.js server actually running? (ps aux | grep node). 3) Does the React App.js have the correct EC2 public IP in the fetch URL? ('http://YOUR_PUBLIC_IP:5000/api/apply' not localhost). 4) Is the CORS middleware enabled in server.js? (app.use(cors())). 5) Is the EC2 instance's public IP the same? (public IPs change if instance is stopped and restarted — use Elastic IP for a permanent address). (Result) Identified and fixed the connectivity issue — most likely port 5000 not open in Security Group.

questions.question: Scenario: An e-commerce company migrates from a self-managed MySQL server to DynamoDB. The old system had complex JOIN queries across orders, products, and customers tables. How do you handle this in DynamoDB?
questions.answer: (Situation) Existing system relies on multi-table JOINs. DynamoDB doesn't support JOINs. (Task) Redesign the data model for DynamoDB. (Action) Apply single-table design: store orders, products, and customer data in ONE DynamoDB table using a hierarchical key structure. Example: Partition Key = 'CUSTOMER#C001', Sort Key = 'PROFILE' stores customer details. Sort Key = 'ORDER#ORD-001' stores order details. Sort Key = 'ORDER#ORD-001#ITEM#PROD-001' stores line items. Query all data for customer C001 with a single Query on Partition Key 'CUSTOMER#C001'. Use GSIs for access patterns like 'all orders by date' or 'all orders by status'. (Result) All JOINs replaced with single DynamoDB queries — lower latency, unlimited scale.

questions.question: Compare DynamoDB On-Demand and Provisioned capacity modes. When would you choose each?
questions.answer: On-Demand: pay per request with instant auto-scaling. No capacity planning needed. Best for: new applications with unknown traffic, spiky or unpredictable workloads, applications with infrequent access (pay nothing when idle). Higher cost per request. Provisioned: pre-set RCU and WCU with optional auto-scaling within defined bounds. Lower cost at sustained load. Best for: established applications with predictable traffic, cost-sensitive workloads at scale, applications needing Reserved Capacity pricing. Rule of thumb: start On-Demand, switch to Provisioned after 30+ days when traffic patterns are understood.

questions.question: What is DynamoDB single-table design and why is it recommended?
questions.answer: Single-table design means storing multiple entity types (users, orders, products) in a single DynamoDB table using carefully crafted partition and sort key patterns. Benefits: 1) Reduces the number of service API calls — one Query can retrieve a customer plus all their orders. 2) Aligns with DynamoDB's strength — it scales per table, not per entity. 3) Eliminates Lambda + DynamoDB latency by batching reads. The trade-off is increased complexity in key design. AWS's own DynamoDB team and Alex DeBrie's 'DynamoDB Book' are the canonical references for this pattern.

questions.question: How does Lambda handle concurrency, and what happens when the concurrency limit is exceeded?
questions.answer: Lambda concurrent execution = number of function instances running simultaneously. Default regional limit: 1,000 concurrent executions (soft limit, increasable). When traffic exceeds this limit, Lambda throttles — new invocations receive TooManyRequestsException (HTTP 429). Mitigation: 1) Request a limit increase via AWS Support. 2) Use Reserved Concurrency to guarantee capacity for critical functions (and cap others). 3) Use SQS as a buffer — messages queue up and Lambda processes at its own rate. 4) Implement exponential backoff and retry in the calling service.

questions.question: Explain DynamoDB Global Tables and the conflict resolution strategy used.
questions.answer: Global Tables create multi-region, multi-active replicas of a DynamoDB table. Writes can occur in any configured AWS region and are automatically replicated to all other regions within seconds (typically under 1 second). Conflict resolution uses last-writer-wins based on timestamps — if two regions write the same item simultaneously, the write with the most recent timestamp wins. Use cases: globally distributed applications needing local low latency, disaster recovery with active-active setup, geo-compliance (data must stay in specific regions with a local replica nearby).

questions.question: What is the difference between DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) and ElastiCache? When would you use each with DynamoDB?
questions.answer: DAX is an in-memory cache purpose-built for DynamoDB — it is DynamoDB-API compatible (no code changes needed, just point to DAX endpoint instead). It caches individual item and query results, reducing read latency from single-digit milliseconds to microseconds. Best for: read-heavy DynamoDB workloads, repeatedly reading the same items. ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) is a general-purpose in-memory cache. Not DynamoDB-specific — requires code changes to check cache before calling DynamoDB. Best for: complex caching logic, session stores, leaderboards (Redis Sorted Sets), or caching results from multiple data sources. Use DAX when you need DynamoDB acceleration with minimal code changes; use ElastiCache for advanced caching patterns beyond simple key lookups.

questions.question: Design a serverless architecture for the Job Application project instead of using EC2. Replace each component with an appropriate AWS serverless service.
questions.answer: Current: EC2 (React) + EC2 (Node.js) + EC2 (MySQL) → All on one T2.medium. Serverless redesign: Frontend: Host the React build as a static website on S3 with CloudFront as CDN — globally distributed, zero servers, costs pennies. Backend: Replace Node.js/Express with API Gateway + Lambda. Each API endpoint becomes a Lambda function (POST /api/apply). File storage: Replace local uploads/ folder with S3 bucket for PDF storage. Lambda writes the PDF to S3 and stores the S3 key in DynamoDB. Database: Replace MySQL with DynamoDB (or RDS Aurora Serverless v2 if SQL is needed). DynamoDB table with applicant details. Benefits: Zero infrastructure management, auto-scales to millions of applications, near-zero cost at low volume, highly available by default. Trade-off: cold starts on Lambda, DynamoDB's NoSQL model replaces SQL queries.
